item.title: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion: Restraint and Raked Sand — Guide
item.description: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion, is the quieter, more contemplative counterpart to the golden Kinkakuji across the city. Built in 1482 as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa and converted to a Zen temple on his death, it was never actually clad in silver — its beauty lies instead in restraint. The dark wooden pavilion overlooks a refined garden of moss, a still pond and, most famously, a great cone of raked white sand and a silvery ‘sea’ meant to reflect the moon.

item.title: Ryoanji: Japan's Most Famous Zen Rock Garden — Guide
item.description: Ryoanji is home to the most famous karesansui, or dry landscape garden, in Japan. Created around the late fifteenth century, it consists of nothing but fifteen rocks set in low moss beds within a rectangle of raked white gravel, enclosed by a low earthen wall. Its fame rests on an enigma: the stones are arranged so that from any vantage point on the viewing veranda, at least one is always hidden behind another.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.
